claims.claim: In 2024, Stonehenge's Altar Stone was traced to Scotland.
claims.source_checked: doi:10.1038/s41586-024-07652-1: full text at https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11324516/; Crossref api.crossref.org/works/10.1038/s41586-024-07652-1 (published online 2024-08-14)
claims.note: Title: 'A Scottish provenance for the Altar Stone of Stonehenge'. Abstract: 'remarkable similarity to the Old Red Sandstone of the Orcadian Basin in northeast Scotland'. Online 14 Aug 2024. 'Traced to' describes what the paper concluded; it is dated, so it does not assert the result still stands.

claims.claim: Now nobody can say exactly where it came from.
claims.source_checked: Crossref works/10.1144/jgs2026-090 (publisher abstract, online 2026-11-05); Crossref works/10.1002/jqs.70080 (publisher abstract, online 2026-06-04); doi:10.14324/AI.27.1.13 full-text PDF https://journals.uclpress.co.uk/ai/article/3293/galley/18572/download/
claims.note: Pirrie 2026 abstract: 'the exact provenance of the Altar Stone is as yet unknown'. Clarke 2026 abstract: 'its source location within this large basin remains unresolved'. Parker Pearson 2024 p.129: 'As yet, the actual outcrop from which the Altar Stone was extracted is unknown'. 'Exactly' keeps it to the source location. Note: the exact outcrop was never known (also not in 2024), so 'Now' marks time, not a loss of a previously exact answer; the sentence is still literally true.

claims.claim: (A4) Hook, as heard by a viewer who swipes away at second two: the Altar Stone was traced to Scotland in 2024, and that finding has since been thrown into doubt (its source is not known exactly).
claims.source_checked: PMC11324516 (Clarke 2024 full text); Crossref abstracts of doi:10.1144/jgs2026-090 and doi:10.1002/jqs.70080
claims.note: First belief is true as dated. Second: Pirrie 2026 (with three of the 2024 authors) says many Orcadian Basin outcrops 'could not have been the source' and that no examined UK ORS outcrop area 'can be shown' to match, so 'in doubt' is fair; Clarke 2026 still favours the Orcadian Basin, so the hook must not (and does not) say the stone is not from Scotland. A viewer who drops 'exactly' and hears 'nobody knows where it came from' would be overstating, but the spoken words do not say that.

claims.claim: The ages of tiny mineral grains inside it matched sandstone in the northeast.
claims.note: U-Pb dating of detrital zircon, apatite and rutile from two Altar Stone fragments; grains 'usually <30 um in width', so 'tiny' holds. Zircon spectra vs Orcadian Basin: Kolmogorov-Smirnov 'fails to reject the null hypothesis that they are derived from the same underlying distribution'; apatite ages from Spittal (Caithness) and Cruaday (Orkney) 'identical, within uncertainty'. The zircon ages are equally indistinguishable from Svalbard ORS, but the line says 'matched', not 'matched only', so it is not overstated. Claims an age match only, so it does not conflict with claim 13.

claims.claim: So how did six tonnes of stone travel more than seven hundred kilometres?
claims.source_checked: PMC11324516 (Clarke 2024 full text); Crossref abstracts of doi:10.1002/jqs.70080 and doi:10.1144/jgs2026-090
claims.note: Figures are right: Clarke 2024 '6 tonne shaped block', 'weighing 6 t', 'at least 750 km'; Clarke 2026 '6000 kg', 'some 700 km'. The problem is the unconditional presupposition. Clarke 2024 states the distance conditionally ('Such a provenance implies that the Altar Stone ... was sourced at least 750 km from its current location'). The script then tells the viewer the source is unresolved, and Pirrie 2026's abstract limits the 2024 grain dating to supporting 'a Laurentian source for the heavy minerals' (not for the rock) and says no examined outcrop area of the UK ORS (not only the Orcadian Basin) can be shown to match, so a basin-level source, and with it the >700 km distance, is not established by that paper. A pedant can ask how the distance is known if the source is not. Change to keep the source's condition, e.g. 'If so, how did six tonnes of stone travel more than seven hundred kilometres?' (or 'From there, ...'), and note in SOURCES entry 3 that the distance holds only for an Orcadian Basin source.

claims.claim: The 2024 team suggested it went by sea.
claims.note: Abstract: 'The difficulty of long-distance overland transport of such massive cargo from Scotland, navigating topographic barriers, suggests that it was transported by sea.' Summary: 'probably by sea'. 'Suggested' keeps the hedge.

claims.claim: But no late Stone Age boat has been found in Britain,
claims.source_checked: doi:10.14324/AI.27.1.13 full-text PDF (UCL Press; 'Published: 31 December 2024'; double-blind peer-reviewed per the PDF; Crossref lists online 2025-01-22)
claims.note: p.128: 'Although no boats are known from the Late Neolithic in Britain or Europe ...'; 'The earliest known boats in Britain ... at Ferriby ... Early Bronze Age sewn-plank boats (Ferriby 3) dates to 2030-1780 cal bc'. 'Late Stone Age' renders 'Late Neolithic'; restricting to Britain is narrower than the source. ('Later Stone Age' is also an African-prehistory term; in context it reads as the period.)

claims.claim: and another study doubts one could carry six tonnes.
claims.note: p.128: 'What we know of Early Bronze Age boats ... would suggest that they and their Late Neolithic precursors were unlikely to be sturdy enough to carry a 6-tonne stone in coastal waters'; a sewn-plank boat for 6 t 'would have to be far greater than the estimated 15 m-16 m length of the Ferriby boats'. 'Doubts' = 'unlikely'. Not false, but note: 'another study' is not independent of the 2024 team (Bevins, Ixer and Pearce are authors of both); line 8 flags shared authors for Pirrie 2026 but not here.

claims.claim: Overland, on a sledge, that study estimates about eight months of hauling.
claims.note: p.128: 'a suitably robust wooden sledge ... sliding on wooden rails'; 'such a journey with a large and heavy sledge could take perhaps four times today's time of under two months ... needing eight months or so to haul a stone from northern Scotland to Stonehenge.' 'Estimates about' matches 'perhaps ... or so'.

claims.claim: A glacier? A 2026 ice model says ice could have carried it part of the way, at most.
claims.source_checked: Crossref works/10.1002/jqs.70080 (publisher-deposited abstract, online 2026-06-04). Wiley full text not opened (bot challenge).
claims.note: Abstract alone states it: 'we combine sandstone provenance analysis with ice flow modelling'; from Caithness a 'localised south-eastward pathway directed towards Dogger Bank'; 'Glacial transport may have provided an intermediate stage in the stone's journey, but alone cannot account for the final emplacement on Salisbury Plain. Even under a glacially assisted scenario, substantial anthropogenic transport would have remained necessary.' 'Could have ... part of the way, at most' does not exceed 'may have provided an intermediate stage'. The abstract's further timing problem (Dogger Bank flooded before the stone likely arrived) only weakens the idea, so 'at most' holds. Clarke 2024 ('difficult to reconcile') and Parker Pearson 2024 ('can be rejected') are harsher; the line is attributed to the 2026 model.

claims.claim: Then, months later, a new study, including three of the 2024 team, looked closer.
claims.source_checked: Crossref works/10.1144/jgs2026-090 (authors, online 2026-11-05, abstract); Crossref works/10.1002/jqs.70080 (online 2026-06-04); Crossref works/10.1038/s41586-024-07652-1 (authors)
claims.note: About five months after the 4 June 2026 ice-model paper. Clarke 2024 authors: Clarke, Kirkland, Bevins, Pearce, Glorie, Ixer. Pirrie 2026 includes Richard E. Bevins, Rob A. Ixer, Nick J. G. Pearce and none of the other three: exactly three. 'Looked closer' = 'a detailed multi-proxy characterization of the sedimentology, geochemistry, detrital and diagenetic mineralogy'.

claims.claim: Many outcrops in that part of Scotland could not have been the source.
claims.source_checked: Crossref works/10.1144/jgs2026-090 (publisher-deposited abstract). Lyell Collection full text not opened (bot challenge).
claims.note: Abstract: 'the overall petrology, heavy mineral assemblage, clay mineralogy and geochemistry show that many outcrops of the Old Red Sandstone (ORS) in the Orcadian Basin could not have been the source of the Altar Stone.' 'That part of Scotland' = the Orcadian Basin of northeast Scotland (line 2; Clarke 2024).

claims.claim: No outcrop examined so far has been shown to match it in every way.
claims.source_checked: Crossref works/10.1144/jgs2026-090 (publisher-deposited abstract); Crossref works/10.1002/jqs.70080 (abstract). Full texts not opened (bot challenge).
claims.note: Pirrie 2026 abstract: 'To date, no examined outcrop area of the UK ORS can be shown to have the same suite of lithological and geochemical characteristics as documented for the Altar Stone.' 'Has been shown to' keeps 'can be shown'; failing the lithological/geochemical suite means no 'match in every way'. The script drops 'of the UK ORS', but no wider match exists either: Clarke 2026 calls the source 'unresolved' and Pirrie 2026 says the exact provenance is 'as yet unknown', which could not be true if any outcrop had been shown to match fully. Optional: 'in Britain' to mirror the abstract's scope.

claims.claim: Where exactly the Altar Stone came from is, for now, unknown.
claims.source_checked: Crossref abstracts of doi:10.1144/jgs2026-090 and doi:10.1002/jqs.70080; doi:10.14324/AI.27.1.13 full-text PDF
claims.note: Pirrie 2026: 'the exact provenance of the Altar Stone is as yet unknown.' Clarke 2026: 'its source location within this large basin remains unresolved'. Parker Pearson 2024: 'As yet, the actual outcrop ... is unknown'. 'For now' = 'as yet'.
